misconceptions.misconception: Matter is simply anything with mass.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly distinguishes matter from mass and presents multiple definitions; mass is a property rather than a substance.

misconceptions.misconception: All matter has a definite everyday size and volume.
misconceptions.correction: Quantum constituents need not have well-defined size or position; apparent spatial occupation emerges from quantum statistics and interactions.

misconceptions.misconception: Mass and matter are conserved in exactly the same sense.
misconceptions.correction: The source's net-matter conservation is framed with baryon/lepton number, while total mass can change as energy changes.

misconceptions.misconception: A phase is the same thing as a thermodynamic state.
misconceptions.correction: Different thermodynamic states can occur within the same phase, such as gases at different pressures.

misconceptions.misconception: Antimatter is automatically outside the concept of matter.
misconceptions.correction: The answer depends on the definition; under the elementary-fermion definition, antimatter constituents are included.

misconceptions.misconception: Most of a nucleon's mass is simply the sum of the bare quark masses.
misconceptions.correction: The source attributes most composite mass to interaction energy associated with gluon fields and quark binding.
The source notes that W and Z bosons are massive while not being classified as ordinary matter under the quark-lepton definition.

questions.question: Why is 'matter' not a single universally accepted technical category?
answers_from_source: Different historical and scientific scales motivate different definitions.
The source uses atomic, proton-neutron-electron, quark-lepton, elementary-fermion, and relativistic energy-momentum perspectives.

questions.question: Why does matter appear to occupy space if elementary particles have no everyday size?
answers_from_source: The source invokes the Pauli exclusion principle and other interactions as mechanisms producing effective spatial separation.

questions.question: Why can most ordinary mass be interaction energy?
answers_from_source: Nucleons contain quarks bound by gluon fields, and the associated field/binding energy contributes most of the nucleon mass.

questions.question: What is the difference between a phase and a thermodynamic state?
answers_from_source: Phase describes a class such as gas; thermodynamic state can differ by pressure, temperature and other state variables within the same phase.

questions.question: Why is antimatter classification definition-dependent?
answers_from_source: One definition identifies matter with quarks/leptons and excludes antiparticles; another identifies matter with elementary fermions and includes antiquarks/antileptons.

questions.question: What does the source mean by conservation of matter?
answers_from_source: It frames net matter using baryon and lepton numbers, which remain conserved in the described processes even when mass-energy changes.

questions.question: How did the concept of matter change historically?
answers_from_source: It shifted from elemental and atomist philosophies to Aristotelian matter/form, Cartesian extension, Newtonian particles, atomic/subatomic structure, and quantum field descriptions.

questions.question: What distinguishes dark matter from ordinary matter?
answers_from_source: Dark matter is inferred gravitationally, is generally treated as non-baryonic, and has unknown microscopic composition.

nodes.label: Matter
nodes.description: A historically and scientifically variable concept referring to physical substance, material content, or, under some definitions, systems composed of fermionic constituents.

nodes.label: Mass
nodes.description: A well-defined extensive property of matter and other physical systems; distinct from the broader and historically variable concept of matter.

nodes.label: Volume
nodes.description: Spatial extent/occupied volume used in the traditional mass-volume-space definition of matter.

nodes.label: Space
nodes.description: Spatial arena or structure relative to which volume, extension, and occupation of space are described.

nodes.label: Rest mass
nodes.description: Mass associated with a system in its rest frame.

nodes.label: Inertial mass
nodes.description: Mass concept associated with resistance to acceleration.

nodes.label: Relativistic mass
nodes.description: Mass terminology referenced by the source as one of several mass notions.

nodes.label: Energy
nodes.description: A conserved physical quantity that can contribute to the mass-energy of systems but is not identical to matter.

nodes.label: Energy–momentum tensor
nodes.description: Tensor used in relativity to characterize the energy, momentum, stresses, and related content of a system; in cosmology it can replace simple rest-mass addition as the quantitative descriptor of matter content.

nodes.label: Atom
nodes.description: Composite quantum system consisting of a nucleus and electrons, in ordinary descriptions.

nodes.label: Molecule
nodes.description: Bound chemical entity composed of atoms; used in several definitions of ordinary matter.

nodes.label: Subatomic particle
nodes.description: Quantum constituent of atoms or other composite systems.

nodes.label: Quantum entity
nodes.description: Entity governed by quantum mechanics rather than classical-object intuitions.

nodes.label: Wave–particle duality
nodes.description: The source's distinction that microscopic matter exhibits both wave-like and particle-like behavior.

nodes.label: Fermion
nodes.description: Particle obeying Fermi–Dirac statistics; elementary fermions in the Standard Model are quarks and leptons.

nodes.label: Boson
nodes.description: Particle class distinct from fermions; force carriers such as photons, W/Z bosons and gluons are bosons.

nodes.label: Quark
nodes.description: Elementary spin-1/2 fermion carrying color charge and fractional electric charge.

nodes.label: Lepton
nodes.description: Elementary spin-1/2 fermion; charged leptons carry electric charge while neutrinos are electrically neutral; leptons lack color charge.

nodes.label: Antiparticle
nodes.description: Particle partner with corresponding quantum numbers of opposite sign where appropriate; ordinary matter and antimatter are related through antiparticle pairing.

nodes.label: Antimatter
nodes.description: Matter-like material composed of antiparticles corresponding to ordinary matter constituents; annihilation can occur when particle-antiparticle pairs interact.

nodes.label: Atomism
nodes.description: Family of ancient particulate theories proposing discrete building blocks of matter.

nodes.label: Chemical substance
nodes.description: A unique form of matter with constant chemical composition and characteristic properties.

nodes.label: Chemical mixture
nodes.description: Combination of two or more chemical substances without chemical reaction, according to the source's chemistry framing.

nodes.label: Phase
nodes.description: Bulk form of matter with relatively uniform chemical composition and physical properties.

nodes.label: Phase transition
nodes.description: Transformation between phases as thermodynamic conditions change.

nodes.label: Thermodynamic state
nodes.description: State characterized by variables such as pressure; distinct from phase identity.

nodes.label: Solid
nodes.description: Classical phase of matter with comparatively fixed shape and structure.

nodes.label: Liquid
nodes.description: Classical phase of matter capable of flow while retaining a condensed state.

nodes.label: Gas
nodes.description: Classical phase of matter that expands to fill available volume.

nodes.label: Plasma
nodes.description: Ionized matter; the source describes it as a gas of ions.

nodes.label: Bose–Einstein condensate
nodes.description: Exotic phase listed by the source.

nodes.label: Fermionic condensate
nodes.description: Exotic phase listed by the source.

nodes.label: Quark–gluon plasma
nodes.description: High-energy form of QCD matter listed as an exotic state.

nodes.label: Superfluid
nodes.description: Exotic phase of matter with collective quantum behavior.

nodes.label: Supersolid
nodes.description: Exotic phase combining solid-like and superfluid-like features.

nodes.label: Magnetic phase
nodes.description: Phase classification including paramagnetic and ferromagnetic states.

nodes.label: Degenerate matter
nodes.description: Low-temperature, high-density fermionic matter whose pressure is governed by quantum statistics and fermion filling.

nodes.label: Fermi energy
nodes.description: Maximum occupied kinetic-energy scale in the zero-temperature idealized fermion gas picture.

nodes.label: Pauli exclusion principle
nodes.description: Principle limiting identical fermions from occupying the same quantum state; invoked as part of the explanation of why matter occupies space.

nodes.label: Baryon
nodes.description: Strongly interacting fermion, typically a three-quark composite; protons and neutrons are baryons.

nodes.label: Meson
nodes.description: Hadron composed of a quark and antiquark; treated in the source as matter-neutral under one baryon/lepton-number classification.

nodes.label: Hadron
nodes.description: Composite particle built from quarks; includes baryons and mesons.

nodes.label: Proton
nodes.description: Baryon found in atomic nuclei, composed of two up quarks and one down quark in the source's quark model.

nodes.label: Neutron
nodes.description: Neutral baryon found in atomic nuclei; composite of quarks.

nodes.label: Atomic nucleus
nodes.description: Dense atomic core composed of protons and neutrons in the source's ordinary atomic picture.

nodes.label: Electron
nodes.description: Charged lepton with spin 1/2 and electric charge -1e.

nodes.label: Neutrino
nodes.description: Electrically neutral lepton with very small mass; source lists electron, muon, and tau neutrinos.

nodes.label: Color charge
nodes.description: Charge associated with the strong interaction carried by quarks.

nodes.label: Electric charge
nodes.description: Electric charge quantum number; quarks have fractional charge, charged leptons have -1e, neutrinos have 0e.

nodes.label: Strong interaction
nodes.description: Fundamental interaction associated with quarks, gluons, color charge, and hadronic binding.

nodes.label: Weak interaction
nodes.description: Fundamental interaction to which quarks and leptons are subject and through which radioactive decay processes occur.

nodes.label: Electromagnetism
nodes.description: Fundamental interaction mediated by photons.

nodes.label: Gravity
nodes.description: Fundamental interaction associated with massive/energetic systems; the source notes its quantum description remains unresolved.

nodes.label: Standard Model
nodes.description: Particle-physics framework used by the source to organize quarks, leptons, gauge bosons, and generations.

nodes.label: Quantum mechanics
nodes.description: Theory governing the quantum nature of microscopic constituents.

nodes.label: General relativity
nodes.description: Relativistic framework in which energy-momentum rather than simple additive rest mass characterizes gravitating systems.

nodes.label: Cosmology
nodes.description: Study of the universe at large scales, including matter, dark matter, dark energy and cosmic expansion.

nodes.label: Astrophysics
nodes.description: Application of physical theory to astronomical objects and phenomena.

nodes.label: Chemistry
nodes.description: Science of substances, composition, properties and transformations of matter.

nodes.label: Nuclear physics
nodes.description: Field concerned with nuclei and nuclear matter/processes.

nodes.label: Particle physics
nodes.description: Field studying elementary particles, their interactions and composite structures.

nodes.label: Condensed matter physics
nodes.description: Field studying collective phases and properties of condensed materials.

nodes.label: Dark matter
nodes.description: Matter of unknown composition inferred through gravitational effects and cosmological evidence; source describes it as predominantly non-baryonic.

nodes.label: Dark energy
nodes.description: Name given to the source of the repulsive influence associated with accelerated cosmic expansion; precise nature is described as unknown.

nodes.label: Exotic matter
nodes.description: Hypothetical forms of matter that may violate one or more properties of known matter; source includes negative-mass possibilities.

nodes.label: Nuclear matter
nodes.description: Matter associated with neutrons and protons and, in generalized form, dense quark matter.

nodes.label: Quark matter
nodes.description: High-density matter described as a liquid of quarks; strange matter is a specific proposed form.

nodes.label: Strange matter
nodes.description: Quark matter containing up, down and strange quarks; narrower usage invokes the hypothesis that it is more stable than nuclear matter.

nodes.label: Strange matter hypothesis
nodes.description: Hypothesis associated with Bodmer and Witten that strange quark matter could be the true ground state of matter.

nodes.label: Baryon number
nodes.description: Quantity assigning +1 to baryons and -1 to antibaryons, with quarks carrying 1/3 in the source's conservation discussion.

nodes.label: Lepton number
nodes.description: Quantity assigning positive number to ordinary leptons and negative number to antileptons in the source's matter-conservation framing.

nodes.label: Conservation of net matter
nodes.description: Source's framing of conservation through baryon and lepton number rather than conservation of total mass.

nodes.label: Mass–energy equivalence
nodes.description: Relationship between mass and energy; invoked in annihilation and binding-energy discussions.

nodes.label: Binding energy
nodes.description: Interaction energy associated with composite systems; source emphasizes its contribution to the mass of hadrons and release in nuclear transformations.

nodes.label: Matter field
nodes.description: Quantum field whose excitations correspond to material particles in field-theoretic descriptions.

nodes.label: Quantum field theory
nodes.description: Framework in which particles are treated as quantum excitations of fields; referenced through matter fields.

nodes.label: Mechanical philosophy
nodes.description: Early modern view treating matter primarily through extension, motion, contact/mechanical behavior.

nodes.label: Hylomorphic matter-form theory
nodes.description: Aristotelian conception in which matter and form are complementary principles underlying substances and change.

nodes.label: Physical ontology
nodes.description: Philosophical inquiry into what physical entities and structures are fundamentally real.

nodes.label: History of the concept of matter
nodes.description: Historical development of definitions of matter as the understood length scale and constituents changed.

Hadronic matter includes baryons.

Gluon-field interaction energy contributes substantially to hadron mass.
Interaction/binding energy contributes to composite mass.

Nonreacting combinations of substances form mixtures.

source_claims.statement: Matter is commonly defined as anything with mass and volume, but the article emphasizes that this definition is not universal across physics.
Everyday matter is commonly described as atoms and things made from atoms, while massless particles such as photons are excluded under that everyday framing.
Quantum mechanics makes the everyday picture of particles as objects with definite size and position only approximately correct.
In the Standard Model, matter is not itself a fundamental concept because elementary constituents lack ordinary size and volume.
Fermionic statistics and fundamental interactions help explain why matter appears to occupy space.
Matter has been conceptualized through particulate theories in ancient Greece and India.
Mass is a property of matter and other systems rather than a substance identical with matter.
The source distinguishes rest mass, inertial mass, and relativistic mass.
Matter exhibits both wave-like and particle-like properties.
In chemistry, a substance is a unique form of matter with constant composition and characteristic properties.
A chemical substance may be an element or compound; nonreacting combinations can form mixtures.
A substance can occupy multiple physical phases without changing chemical composition.
One matter definition identifies matter with atoms; this can be extended to charged atoms/molecules and plasma/electrolytes.
A finer-grained definition identifies matter with protons, neutrons, and electrons, thereby including electron beams and white-dwarf matter.

source.section: Based on protons, neutrons and electrons

source_claims.statement: A still finer definition identifies ordinary matter with quarks and leptons.
Most everyday mass is attributed to interaction energy associated with the binding of quarks inside nucleons rather than simply the bare quark masses.
The Standard Model groups quarks and leptons into three generations.
Mass is not exclusive to ordinary matter because W/Z bosons can be massive without being classified as ordinary matter under the quark-lepton definition.
A broad elementary-fermion definition includes antimatter because antiquarks and antileptons are also fermions.
In relativity, the energy-momentum tensor is more general than simply adding rest masses of components.
In cosmological usage, matter may mean anything contributing to the energy-momentum of a system, with the source noting that this can include light and massless fields.
Quarks are spin-1/2 fermions with fractional electric charge and color charge.
Baryons are strongly interacting fermions; protons and neutrons are examples.
The source distinguishes baryonic, hadronic, degenerate, nuclear, quark, and strange forms of matter.
Degenerate matter is governed by Fermi statistics and exclusion; at low temperature its pressure depends strongly on fermion number.
Chandrasekhar's white-dwarf mass limit is presented as a major consequence of degeneracy physics.
Strange matter has a broad meaning as three-flavor quark matter and a narrower meaning as potentially more stable than nuclear matter.
Leptons are spin-1/2 fermions; charged leptons carry -1e while neutrinos are electrically neutral and leptons have no color charge.
Phases are bulk forms of matter with relatively uniform composition and physical properties; phase depends on ambient pressure, temperature and volume.
Phase and thermodynamic state are distinct: different pressures can produce different thermodynamic states within the same gas phase.
Antimatter is described as matter composed of antiparticles of ordinary matter constituents, but whether it is called matter depends on the adopted definition.
Particle-antiparticle annihilation can convert rest mass into other particles and kinetic energy consistent with mass-energy equivalence.
The article identifies the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe as an unresolved problem and relates it to CP violation and baryogenesis.
The source's conservation framing uses baryon and lepton number rather than conservation of total mass.
Nuclear reactions release binding energy while baryon number remains conserved.
Electron-positron annihilation does not change net matter under the baryon/lepton-number definition because initial net lepton number is zero.
Ordinary matter is described as a small fraction of the observable-universe energy budget, with dark matter and dark energy comprising the remainder in the cited cosmological model.
Dark matter is inferred gravitationally and is commonly modeled as predominantly non-baryonic.
Dark energy is associated with accelerated cosmic expansion and its physical nature is described as unknown.
Exotic matter is a hypothetical category that may include properties outside known matter, such as negative mass.
The concept of matter has been repeatedly refined as knowledge of constituents and interactions changed.
The source frames the history of matter as a history of the length scales and building blocks used to define it.
Indian traditions proposed atoms/paramanu or pudgala, with different schools incorporating distinct philosophical commitments.
Greek pre-Socratic thinkers proposed different fundamental substances or principles, including water, apeiron, air, fire, four elements, and atomism.
Aristotle treated matter and form as complementary principles and tied matter intrinsically to change and becoming.
Descartes defined matter as extended substance and developed a mechanical philosophy contrasting matter with mind.
Newton inherited the mechanical conception but assigned matter additional intrinsic properties and used gravity in a way that challenged strict contact mechanics.
Priestley argued for inherent powers of matter beyond contact mechanics, including chemical attraction.
Nineteenth-century chemistry and atomic theory increasingly treated atoms as constituents of molecules and compounds.
The electron, atomic nucleus, and particle physics shifted the conception of matter toward subatomic structure.
Modern field-theoretic descriptions speak of particles as quantum excitations of matter fields.
The source states that gravity remains unaccounted for at the quantum level within the Standard Model framework.
The article supplies an extensive bibliography spanning philosophy, chemistry, particle physics, cosmology, condensed matter and astrophysics.
The article includes further reading on the historical and philosophical concept of matter and on elementary particles.

historical_timeline.description: Indian philosophical tradition proposes discrete atoms/paramanu as building blocks of matter.
Greek thinkers propose water, apeiron, air, fire, four elements and atomism as accounts of underlying matter.
Aristotle treats matter and form as complementary principles underlying substance and change.
Descartes identifies extension as the nature of bodily substance and develops mechanical philosophy.
Newton develops a particle-based conception with extension, hardness, impenetrability, mobility and inertia.
Priestley argues that matter possesses intrinsic powers such as chemical attraction.
Periodic classification and atomic theory make atoms central to explanations of molecules and compounds.
Discovery of the electron and later the atomic nucleus shifts matter theory toward subatomic constituents.
Particle physics reframes matter in terms of elementary quarks and leptons and their interactions.
Particles are described as quantum excitations of matter fields.
Quantum degeneracy becomes central to white dwarf and neutron star matter; Chandrasekhar's mass limit is highlighted.
Bodmer proposes that strange quark matter might be more stable than ordinary nuclear matter.
Witten develops a strange-matter scenario in cosmological phase-transition context.
Galaxy dynamics and cosmological evidence motivate a non-baryonic dark matter component.
Accelerated cosmic expansion is modeled using a dark-energy component with unknown physical nature.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Matter is a category/concept about physical substance or material content; mass is a quantitative physical property that can also characterize systems not classified as matter.
Matter is not identical to energy; interaction/binding energy contributes to composite mass, and energy can exist in forms not classified as matter.
Matter is a broad physical-science concept, whereas chemical substance denotes a chemically defined form with constant composition and characteristic properties.
A phase is a class of bulk matter with relatively uniform properties; thermodynamic state can vary within a phase, such as different-pressure gases.
The quark-lepton definition is narrower than a general elementary-fermion definition because the latter also includes antiquarks and antileptons.
Baryonic matter is a subset/convenient category centered on baryons; ordinary matter may be defined more broadly in terms of quarks and leptons.
Antimatter consists of antiparticle constituents; classification as matter or as the opposite of matter depends on the definition used.
The source's net-matter conservation is expressed through baryon/lepton number, while total mass can change through energy release and annihilation processes.
Under the source's ordinary-matter definition, quarks/leptons are matter constituents while gauge bosons mediate forces and are not classified as ordinary matter, despite some being massive.
Classical intuition assigns definite size/position; quantum entities exhibit wave-particle behavior and need not possess everyday size or position.
Nuclear matter is described in terms of nucleons; strange matter contains up, down and strange quarks and may, under a stronger hypothesis, be more stable than nuclear matter.
Dark matter is inferred from gravitational effects and contributes matter-like mass-energy; dark energy is invoked to explain accelerated cosmic expansion.
